findings.title: Missing CSRF protection for state-changing operations
findings.description: The Flask application has no CSRF token validation for POST/DELETE endpoints. All state-changing operations in /api/decisions, /api/bulk-decisions, and /api/decisions/<id> are vulnerable to cross-site request forgery attacks. An attacker could trick a logged-in user into submitting decisions or deleting review data via malicious links or embedded forms.
findings.code_snippet:
# No Flask-WTF or CSRF protection configured
app = Flask(__name__)
app.config.from_object(config_class)
# Missing: csrf = CSRFProtect(app)
findings.recommendation: Install Flask-WTF and enable CSRF protection: (1) Add 'flask-wtf>=1.2.0' to requirements.txt, (2) Add 'csrf = CSRFProtect(app)' in create_app(), (3) Update templates to include {{ csrf_token() }}, (4) Configure CSRF exemptions for health check endpoint if needed. Note: This will break existing AJAX calls until they are updated to include CSRF tokens.

findings.title: Missing security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options, HSTS)
findings.description: The application does not set any security headers. Missing: Content-Security-Policy (allows inline scripts, XSS risk), X-Frame-Options (clickjacking risk), X-Content-Type-Options (MIME sniffing risk), Strict-Transport-Security (HTTPS enforcement). This leaves the application vulnerable to XSS, clickjacking, and MIME-based attacks.
findings.code_snippet: # No security headers configured in create_app() or middleware
findings.recommendation: Add Flask-Talisman for security headers: (1) pip install flask-talisman, (2) In create_app(): Talisman(app, content_security_policy={'default-src': "'self'", 'script-src': ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"], 'style-src': ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"]}, force_https=False in development). Note: May need to adjust CSP policy based on actual inline script/style usage. Consider removing 'unsafe-inline' by extracting inline JavaScript to external files.

findings.title: Weak SECRET_KEY default allows session manipulation
findings.description: Config class uses 'dev-secret-key-not-for-production' as SECRET_KEY default. While production config validates SECRET_KEY is set, development and testing configs use this weak default. If the app is accidentally deployed in development mode or if an attacker discovers this default is in use, they can forge session cookies and impersonate users (once authentication is added).
findings.recommendation: Generate strong SECRET_KEY for all environments: (1) Remove default from Config class, (2) Require SECRET_KEY in .env for all modes, (3) Update .env.template with generation command: SECRET_KEY=$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))'), (4) Add startup validation in all config classes to raise error if SECRET_KEY is missing or matches known weak defaults.

findings.title: DEBUG mode enabled in DevelopmentConfig and TestingConfig
findings.description: DEBUG=True is hardcoded in DevelopmentConfig and TestingConfig (lines 42, 49). If the app is deployed with APP_ENV=development by mistake, detailed error messages with stack traces would be exposed to users, leaking sensitive information about file paths, database schema, and internal logic. This aids attackers in reconnaissance.
findings.recommendation: Add environment detection safeguards: (1) Create a prod-check script that verifies APP_ENV=production on deployment, (2) Add startup warning in create_app() if DEBUG=True and DATABASE_URL looks like production (doesn't contain 'localhost' or 'test'), (3) Consider adding an APP_ENV validator that rejects development mode if HTTPS is detected or if a PRODUCTION_MODE env var is set.

findings.title: No authentication/authorization system - unrestricted access
findings.description: The application has no authentication or authorization. Anyone with network access can view all filings, submit/delete review decisions, and access the entire database via the web interface. There is no audit trail for who made what changes (session IDs are tracked, but not tied to user identity). This is acceptable for single-user local deployment but dangerous if exposed to network.
findings.code_snippet: # No authentication decorators, no login routes, no user model
findings.recommendation: If multi-user deployment is planned: (1) Add Flask-Login for session management, (2) Create users table with bcrypt password hashing, (3) Add login/logout routes, (4) Protect all /review and /api routes with @login_required decorator, (5) Add reviewer_id foreign key to review_decisions table, (6) Implement role-based access control if needed (admin vs reviewer). For single-user: Document that the app should only run on localhost or behind reverse proxy with authentication.

findings.title: No API rate limiting - vulnerable to abuse
findings.description: API endpoints (/api/decisions, /api/bulk-decisions) have no rate limiting. An attacker could flood the application with bulk decision requests, causing database overload or denial of service. The SEC client has rate limiting (100ms between requests), but web API does not.
findings.recommendation: Add Flask-Limiter: (1) pip install flask-limiter, (2) In create_app(): limiter = Limiter(app, key_func=get_remote_address, default_limits=['200 per hour']), (3) Apply to API routes: @limiter.limit('100 per hour') for /api/decisions, (4) Stricter limit for bulk: @limiter.limit('20 per hour') for /api/bulk-decisions, (5) Add rate limit headers to responses for transparency. Consider Redis-backed storage for distributed deployments.

findings.title: XSS risk from |safe filter in templates (mitigated by proper escaping)
findings.description: The review.html template uses the |safe filter 5 times (lines 275, 295, 306, 326, 336) to render highlighted context and HTML content. Review of _highlight_context() and _highlight_html() confirms both functions properly escape user input using markupsafe.escape() before adding HTML markup. However, this creates a maintenance risk - if these functions are modified incorrectly, XSS vulnerabilities could be introduced.
findings.recommendation: Add security tests: (1) Create unit tests for _highlight_context() and _highlight_html() that verify XSS payloads like '<script>alert(1)</script>' are properly escaped, (2) Add test cases for edge cases: number/keyword containing HTML entities, quotes, angle brackets, (3) Document in function docstrings that these functions must maintain XSS protection, (4) Consider adding a security code review checklist for any changes to these functions. Risk is LOW because current implementation is correct.

findings.title: SQL injection protection verified - all queries parameterized
findings.description: Comprehensive review of src/infra/db.py (4,006 lines) confirms all SQL queries use parameterized queries with %s placeholders. No f-strings, .format(), or string concatenation found in SQL construction. The db.execute() method properly passes parameters separately. Psycopg3 handles parameterization correctly. This is a POSITIVE finding - no vulnerabilities detected.
findings.code_snippet:
# Example of correct parameterization:
cur.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM companies WHERE cik = %s",
    (cik,)
)
findings.recommendation: No action required. Consider adding a pre-commit hook or CI check using semgrep/bandit to detect SQL injection patterns (f"SELECT", execute(.*+.*), etc.) to prevent future regressions. Add to CLAUDE.md: 'All SQL queries MUST use parameterized queries - never f-strings or concatenation.'

findings.title: Path traversal protection implemented in file operations
findings.description: FilingFetcher._get_storage_dir() (lines 91-128) properly validates CIK and accession_number to prevent path traversal attacks. Checks for '../', '/', '\' characters before constructing file paths. Similar validation exists in validation.py for validate_cik() and validate_accession_number(). This is a POSITIVE finding.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Consider using pathlib.Path.resolve() + .is_relative_to() as additional defense-in-depth for new file operations. Document in CLAUDE.md: 'All user-controlled file paths MUST be validated for path traversal before use.'

findings.title: No secret leakage in logging detected
findings.description: Grep search for logger.*(api_key|password|secret|token|credential) found no matches where secrets are logged. The openai_client.py logs warnings about tiktoken but does not log API keys. sec_client.py logs request timing but not credentials. This is a POSITIVE finding.
findings.code_snippet: # No secret logging found in codebase
findings.recommendation: Add documentation: Create a security.md file documenting: (1) Secrets MUST NOT be logged at any level, (2) Exception messages should be sanitized before logging if they might contain credentials, (3) Add pre-commit hook to scan for common secret patterns (api_key=, password=, token=) in code. Consider adding a secrets scanner like truffleHog or git-secrets to CI.

findings.title: Missing input validation for text field lengths in API
findings.description: While API validation checks for max length on reviewer_notes (1000 chars) and rejection_reason (500 chars), there's no validation on assigned_metric_id string length or rejection_category length. An attacker could submit extremely long strings causing database errors or buffer issues. The database may have column constraints, but API should validate first.
findings.recommendation: Add max length validation: (1) In _validate_assigned_metric_id(): add check 'if len(value) > 50: return "Must be 50 characters or less"', (2) Add length validation for rejection_category (currently only checks enum membership), (3) Add validation for decision field (currently only checks enum), (4) Consider using Pydantic RequestModel classes for automatic validation.

findings.title: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=False allows session hijacking over HTTP
findings.description: Config base class sets SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=False (line 29), meaning session cookies are sent over unencrypted HTTP connections. Only ProductionConfig overrides to True. If the app is deployed with development config or accessed via HTTP in production, session cookies could be intercepted via man-in-the-middle attacks.
findings.code_snippet: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False  # Set True in production with HTTPS
findings.recommendation: Enforce HTTPS: (1) Set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True in base Config class, (2) Add HTTPS redirect middleware for production, (3) Update development config to use HTTPS (self-signed cert or mkcert), (4) Add startup warning if SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=False and app is not running on localhost. Consider using Flask-Talisman's force_https=True for production.

findings.title: No dependency vulnerability scanning in CI
findings.description: Requirements.txt has no version pinning for patch releases, and there's no automated dependency vulnerability scanning (safety, pip-audit) in the development workflow. The project could unknowingly use packages with known CVEs.
findings.code_snippet:
# No pinned versions, only minimum versions:
psycopg[binary,pool]>=3.1.0
requests>=2.31.0
findings.recommendation: Add security scanning: (1) Pin major.minor versions, allow patch: 'requests~=2.31.0' (allows 2.31.x), (2) Add to requirements-dev.txt: 'safety>=3.0.0', 'pip-audit>=2.6.0', (3) Add pre-commit hook: 'safety check --json', (4) Add CI job: 'pip-audit --require-hashes' (requires hashes in requirements.txt), (5) Enable Dependabot in GitHub for automated security updates. Consider quarterly manual review of dependency updates.

findings.title: Error handlers expose generic messages but log full details
findings.description: Error handlers in _register_error_handlers() (lines 356-370) return generic 'Internal server error' messages to users while logging full exception details. This is CORRECT behavior - avoids information disclosure while enabling debugging. However, the 500 error handler doesn't check if DEBUG=True before rendering detailed error page.
findings.recommendation: Verify 500.html template doesn't include {{ error }} variable that could leak exception details. If it does, remove or only display when app.debug=True. Add test case: Trigger 500 error in production config and verify response doesn't contain file paths, SQL queries, or internal variable names. This is LOW severity because the code structure is correct - just needs verification.

findings.title: Audit log captures IP addresses without privacy policy
findings.description: The audit log system (review.py:37-109, api.py:33-115) captures IP addresses, user agents, and session IDs for all requests. While this is valuable for security monitoring, there's no documented privacy policy or data retention strategy. GDPR/CCPA may require disclosure and retention limits.
findings.recommendation: Add privacy documentation: (1) Create privacy.md documenting what data is collected and why, (2) Add audit log retention policy: 'Logs are retained for 90 days, then purged', (3) Create cleanup script: DELETE FROM review_audit_log WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days', (4) Add to CLAUDE.md: 'Audit logs must not contain PII beyond IP/session ID', (5) If deployed in EU/CA: Add privacy banner to UI. For internal-only deployment, document that GDPR doesn't apply.

summary: Security review identified 15 findings across 6 categories. CRITICAL (2): Weak SECRET_KEY defaults and DEBUG mode hardcoded in non-production configs. HIGH (3): Missing CSRF protection, no security headers, no API rate limiting. MEDIUM (4): No authentication system, session cookies over HTTP, missing input length validation, no dependency scanning. LOW (6): Includes 4 positive findings where security is correctly implemented (SQL injection protection, path traversal prevention, no secret logging, XSS protection). The application has solid fundamentals (parameterized queries, input validation) but lacks critical web security protections (CSRF, CSP, rate limiting) needed for production deployment. Most issues can be addressed with configuration changes and adding Flask security extensions (Flask-WTF, Flask-Talisman, Flask-Limiter).
